newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: World trade ministers battle over labour rights.
newsitem.headline: World trade ministers battle over labour rights.

text.p: World trade ministers debated down to the wire on Thursday over the vexed question of whether the World Trade Organisation (WTO) should be involved in improving standards for workers.
Pakistan declared victory in the battle to keep a link between international trade and labour standards out of the final declaration of the WTO's first ministerial conference, which ends on Friday.
However, WTO spokesman Keith Rockwell said a deal was still likely, although he would not say what it might be.

Pakistani Commerce Minister Mohammed Zubair Khan told reporters the conference chairman, Singapore Trade Minister Yeo Cheow Tong, had assured him that the issue would not be in the final declaration, effectively the WTO agenda.
"This has been a great victory for developing countries and all of those who supported us," Khan said.
Conference sources said earlier in the debate that the United States, the main force behind insistence that labour rights be included, had threatened to block a final declaration if it was not.
There was no immediate comment on the state of the debate from U.S. officials.

Washington, supported by some European nations, including France, insists voters' concerns over 250 million child labourers, mostly in the developing world, and sweatshop conditions must be tackled to maintain public support for global free trade.
A large group of ministers was due to meet again later on Thursday on this and other hitches holding up the declaration.
A full meeting of all the ministers was not scheduled until Friday morning. "We hope to carry the rest of the people with us," Khan said.
India and Malaysia, two other nations that have been insistent there should be no mention of labour rights in the final declaration, declined to declare victory, but were clearly happy.
Indian Commerce Minister B.B. Ramaiah told Reuters he was reasonably satisfied the issue would not appear in the final declaration.
Malaysia's Rafidah Aziz left the talks glowing. Asked how the negotiations on the labour issue were going, she replied. "Very good. I'm very happy, you see I'm smiling." She declined further comment.
Rockwell conceded that agreement on the declaration was unlikely on Thursday and that the workers' rights issue was the biggest outstanding issue.
However, the ministers were all showing flexibility, he said, adding that he was sure of a final declaration.
Opponents, mostly Asian, said they saw the U.S. push as an attempt to use the WTO trade disputes procedures to undermine the competitive advantage of low-cost labour in developing nations.
They say the issue should remain the sole concern of the International Labour Organisation (ILO), which was set up to deal with labour standards.
